rule: These profiles are analysis labels, not imitation instructions. Never copy recognizable lyrics, melodies, voices, or signature flows.

profiles.translation: Use dense rhyme only when meaning stays clear and the drums support it.
Favor natural melodic speech and direct emotion; keep phrases fully original.
Let restraint, tone, and repetition carry weight instead of overwriting.
Test short repeatable cells and unusual but natural melodic shapes.
Use rhythmic surprise only where the drum pattern invites it.
Use emotionally important held vowels selectively and keep the range performable.
Let rests and tone do work instead of adding filler.
Prioritize lines that sound normal aloud and clean section transitions.
Keep technical writing understandable and make each verse progress the idea.
Use perspective or cadence changes only when they deepen the concept.
Use fragments and repeated motifs when tone and groove can carry meaning.
Treat vocal texture and silence as arrangement without copying recognizable effects.
Keep verses grounded, readable, and meaning-first.
Use structural surprise only when the concept benefits from it.
Use a simple central thesis and let arrangement create scale.
Blend techniques only when the beat supports them and keep the hook simple.
Prioritize clear melodic identity and section contrast.
Allow imperfect sentence shapes and slant rhyme if they feel true.
Use concrete scenes and leave interpretive space instead of explaining everything.
Keep lines cool and concise when tone can carry the emotion.
Favor plainspoken specificity over ornamental wording.
Use clean melodic cells and clear verse-to-hook contrast.
Let the chorus state the emotional truth more simply than the verses.
Use clear section roles and purposeful rhythmic changes.
Choose phrases that are easy to recognize after one listen.
Use singable endings and leave harmonic room for layers.
Make the title effortless to sing and keep the groove central.
Use a strong central phrase and let arrangement create drama.
Use fewer attacks and let quiet delivery create tension.
Use concrete verse details and a simple emotionally decisive chorus.
Let details earn the chorus and use callbacks with changed meaning.
Keep stories easy to follow and choruses simpler than verses.
Let dynamics amplify a concise chorus rather than adding words.
Give rhythmic verses and melodic hooks clearly different jobs.
Use theatrical structure only when the concept earns it; keep lines natural.
Keep the chorus plain and immediate; let guitars provide scale.
Allow wit in verses but keep the chorus easy to remember.
Prefer simple spoken language and fast-clean section contrast.
Use restrained setup and a larger chorus without overcrowding it.
Make the hook easy to say and easy to remember.
Let the band answer the vocal and reserve density for the build.
Use few core phrases and let melody/arrangement create scale.
Use precise observations and natural rhythmic speech without forced poetry.
Let small lyrical cells repeat while production carries evolution.
Use everyday detail and make the title feel inevitable by the chorus.
Leave room for vocal tone and avoid overcomplicating the lyric.
Use concrete scenes and make Verse 2 add a consequence.
Use one sharp observation instead of several decorative lines.

aggregate_lessons: Dense technical verses work best when hooks get simpler.
Melodic genres benefit from vowel-friendly endings more than perfect rhyme.
Minimalist writers make silence and tone part of the composition.
Story-focused writers use Verse 2 to add consequence, not repeat premise.
Rock and pop-punk rely heavily on dynamic contrast between verse and chorus.
Modern rap often uses repetition as groove, with cadence and production creating progression.
Strong pop writing usually gives the listener one obvious phrase to remember.
Specific everyday details often feel more human than abstract emotional language.
Artist reference should influence craft selection, never wording or melody replication.
